item.title: U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
item.description:
A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.
The 41-year-old suspect hasn't been publicly identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
The officer was caught in a sting operation and arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, the official said. He is expected to be charged Sunday or Monday.
The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and that the force was carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.
The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.
"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security."
FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

item.title: Pope declares Peru his "homeland" in final leg of South America trip
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV declared Peru his "homeland" on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party erupted to welcome the beloved "Padre Robert" home.
Leo seemed genuinely moved as he emerged from his charter plane, smiling broadly at nearly every turn of his first moments on Peruvian soil. The Vatican estimated that some 3 million people lined Leo's miles-long motorcade route into town, waving Peruvian and Holy See flags.
Some in the roaring crowds broke through the tight security to chase behind the car that transported him to the presidential palace, where Leo met privately with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. During the formal welcome ceremony in the palace courtyard, he sang the Peruvian national anthem alongside Fujimori and a children's choir.
Pope Leo waves to the faithful from the popemobile on his way to Peru's government palace in Lima on Nov. 11, 2026.
Miguel Marruffo /AFP via Getty Images
In his first remarks to Fujimori and government officials, the Chicago-born Leo said the Peruvian citizenship he acquired in 2015 cemented a bond that began long before, crediting Peruvians with having formed him as a pastor by sharing their lives, joys and struggles with him.
"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said.
"That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he said to applause.
Popemania descends on Peru, where Leo lived and served for decades

item.title: Trump says "we don't need a deal with Iran"
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: "We don't need a deal with Iran," President Trump declared Thursday in a social media post, hours after he again declared victory in the war during a Veterans Day address, but acknowledged the conflict wasn't over. "Just a question of when we want to end it," he said.A senior Iranian security official insisted Thursday that Tehran would "decide on the manner and agenda of any negotiations" with the U.S. only after its "seven conditions are fulfilled and accepted." Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called those conditions "unacceptable."The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council vowed Wednesday that Tehran would not allow the removal of "even a single particle of enriched nuclear material" from the country, casting doubt on diplomatic efforts as the U.S. has long sought a peace deal that would see Iran give up its enriched uranium.
New Updates
2:26 PM
Iran claims U.S. asked Russia to mediate deal
Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, told Al Jazeera that U.S. officials requested that Russian President Vladimir Putin facilitate negotiations between the country and Iran.
"It was the Americans who, during a visit to Moscow, spoke with Mr. Putin and asked him to speak with Iran so that, in any case, Iran would agree to speak directly with them," Qalibaf said.
The White House did not directly respond to the Associated Press' query about whether the U.S. has asked Putin to facilitate talks with Iran.

item.title: What to know as "super El Niño" conditions take shape
item.description:
El Niño has become especially powerful this year, with "super El Niño" conditions now officially taking shape.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center announced Thursday that the phenomenon, which affects weather and climate around the world, has intensified and continues to strengthen. Its effects through next spring may even be considered historic, the agency said.
Here's everything to know about El Niño:
What is El Niño?
El Niño is a climate pattern defined by warming waters in a specific region of the Pacific Ocean near the equator. It occurs every two to seven years and usually lasts between nine and 12 months.
When El Niño is active, a large portion of the world gets warmer, too. In September, researchers at the University of Chicago predicted that an estimated 451,000 more people would die worldwide during this year's El Niño, compared with a typical year, because of excessive heat exposure.
The impacts of El Niño vary in different parts of the world, adjusting hurricane frequencies, altering sea levels, and at times triggering mass flooding or severe drought as well as seasonal snowfall amounts that depart from historical averages.
This graphic illustrates El Niño's impact on winter weather in the U.S.
CBS News
Fishing and agricultural industries often feel tangible consequences of those changes, as do utilities that depend on rainfall and wind to generate power.
A "super" El Niño

item.title: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom
item.description:
Ulanqab, China — Off a major highway on the outskirts of Ulanqab, in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia, Hereford cows roam through corn fields scouring the ground for any dried up remains of the recent harvest.
Hovering over the landscape are shiny new transmission towers linked by power cables that stretch along the plateau for as far as the eye can see. On the ridgeline, covered in snow, wind turbines spin, taking full advantage of the ever-blowing wind.
The energy pulsing from the remote Chinese region — a combination of renewables and fossil fuels — will soon power multi-story data centers being constructed on farmland as part of a sprawling AI data center construction boom.
The construction site is the size of a small American city. It is the biggest, and fastest growing infrastructure project anywhere in China right now.
An image from video broadcast by Chinese state television on Oct. 16, 2026, shows data centers, some still under construction, in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China.
CCTV/Reuters
This corner of Inner Mongolia was famous for generations for growing potatoes. Now, it's fast becoming an AI hub, and Chinese officials hope the expansive, rugged landscape will help power the country's ambition to surpass the U.S. as the global leader in artificial intelligence.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in wake of affair, China spy scandal
Baletu, a 72-year-old farmer, who has lived here for more than 40 years growing potatoes and corn, said the changes across his local landscape are positive.
"It doesn't affect my farmland, not at all," he told CBS News. "It's good for the area."

item.title: Ukraine says Starshield throttled again as U.S. pushes for a deal
item.description:
As President Trump's senior envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed Thursday in a snowy Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said connection issues with the Starlink satellite network were again affecting his country's ability to defend itself from incoming Russian missiles and drones.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces using Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink network, which was also impacted last month, were again facing a "systemic speed restriction."
Ukrainian interceptors, used to shoot down Russian weapons, have been losing their Starshield satellite guidance connection this week if they try to fly faster than about 100 miles per hour.
"Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant malfunctions in Starshield's operation over Ukraine's territory for several days now: along the entire front line and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory," Zelenskyy said in a social media post. "Ukrainian military personnel have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but a systemic speed restriction. For us, this primarily means a significant increase in the difficulty of intercepting Russian jet-powered drones."
A Ukrainian official confirmed the restrictions to CBS News, saying "the speed limitations as of now are on Ukrainian occupied territories and across the contact line. The contact line is the first line of our defense and the first point for interception of Russian drones. It started gradually 3 days ago and now it's 100%."

item.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6, health authorities say
item.description:
An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people and wounded at least a dozen more, Gaza's Health Ministry said Thursday. The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck "a senior Hamas terrorist" and other militants "while they were operating within Nasser Hospital," without providing evidence.
Israel accuses Hamas and its allies of using hospitals as cover for military activity.
In the statement, the Israeli military said Hamas was using the hospital as "a command center for military and terrorist activities."
A Palestinian man inspects damage inside a building at Nasser Hospital following an Israeli airstrike in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, on Nov. 12, 2026.
Ramadan Abed/REUTERS
The Hamas-controlled Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgery department and that a doctor was among the dead. An Associated Press journalist at the scene said parts of the building's second floor were destroyed.
Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in the Palestinian territory, where healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by the yearslong war.
Israeli forces have previously attacked and raided Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed five journalists — including AP contributor Mariam Dagga — when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex.
The war started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-r...

item.title: Company under scrutiny for ties to Nvidia and China
item.description:
The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned.
In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.
And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.
Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.
Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In a statement Thursday, Megaspeed said it "takes its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously" and that it's "committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government."

item.title: China fines a company over a Dove chocolate "situationship" ad
item.description:
Chinese authorities have fined a company the equivalent of about $120,000 over an advertisement it created for American chocolate brand Dove that featured a woman in a "situationship," saying on Thursday it promoted the "wrong views on marriage and relationships."
The video, first posted online in August, showed a woman getting chocolates from a man with whom she was in a "situationship" after her boyfriend ignored her.
The clip caused a stir online in China, with some social media users saying it promoted infidelity, prompting Dove to issue an apology.
Zongzheng Food — the company that created the ad and that operates a Dove store on Chinese e-commerce platform Kuaishou — was fined 800,000 yuan ($120,000) last month, Shanghai authorities said on Thursday.
The ad "packaged being unfaithful in a relationship as a 'sweet experience,' promoting wrong views on marriage and relationships and violating good social customs," the Shanghai Municipal Market Supervision Administration said in a statement.
China is facing a demographic crisis after its birth rate halved over the past decade, and in response authorities have heavily promoted traditional family structures.
Marriage registrations from January to September were down 9.8% year-over-year, reaching just 4.6 million, data from China's civil affairs ministry showed last week.
Dove, which is owned by McLean, Virginia-based Mars Inc., said in its apology in August that the ad didn't follow its content review process and was "clearly inappropriate."
Dove "bears responsibility" for all content posted to its official channels, the chocolate brand said on social media platform Weibo.
Chinese authorities have previously rebuked companies for platforming romantic relationships deemed inappropriate.
In May, Chinese consumer electronics company OPPO said it "severely punished" multiple executives over an ad joking about infidelity, which authorities publicly condemned.

item.title: Nvidia's board preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang, sources say
item.description: The board of Nvidia, the world's largest artificial intelligence chipmaker whose stock makes up a major portion of many retirement programs, is preparing to force out its CEO after his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, sources told CBS News. Kelly O'Grady reports on the latest for the $4 trillion company.
